central_question: Why does toast sometimes burn even when the timer says “done”?
hook: A toaster pops up a golden slice, but the timer’s green light blinks off and the bread is already blackened. How can a machine that’s supposed to stop heating still scorch your toast?
aha_moment: The toaster’s timer only measures time, not color – the heating element stays hot for seconds after the switch trips, pushing the Maillard reaction past its sweet spot into caramelization and then pyrolysis.

story_arc.purpose: Introduce the mystery and promise a concrete answer
story_arc.reveal: We see a perfectly timed toast that ends up charred, raising the question of what the timer actually controls.
required_facts: Toast pops up, timer lights off, bread is burnt

story_arc.purpose: Explain the common assumption and reveal the real timer type
story_arc.reveal: Most people think the timer senses color, but it’s a thermal‑time switch (bimetallic strip or capacitor) that simply counts seconds.
required_facts: Timer is a mechanical/electrical switch, not a sensor

story_arc.purpose: Show element temperature and thermal inertia
story_arc.reveal: Nichrome wires glow at >1400 °C and stay above 200 °C for 1–2 s after power cuts, radiating heat that keeps browning the bread.

story_arc.purpose: Detail the Maillard window and post‑timer burn
story_arc.reveal: Golden brown forms at 140–180 °C; beyond 200 °C sugars caramelize then pyrolyze, turning black. The element’s residual heat pushes the surface past this window.

story_arc.purpose: Midpoint reversal – the timer’s lag depends on kitchen temperature
story_arc.reveal: In a cold kitchen the bimetallic strip takes longer to bend, extending heating time and making toast darker, while a hot kitchen shortens it.
required_facts: Bimetallic bend time varies with ambient temperature

story_arc.purpose: Explain capacitor‑based timer overshoot and bread‑specific factors
story_arc.reveal: Capacitors keep the element on until voltage drops, adding a brief overshoot. High‑sugar or thin slices reach burn temperature faster, so the same setting can over‑cook them.

story_arc.purpose: Show residual heat effect and debunk myths
story_arc.reveal: A second slice in a recently used toaster gets extra heat from warm walls, often burning even on a low setting. Higher settings don’t mean more power, just longer time.
required_facts: Residual heat, higher setting = longer time

story_arc.purpose: Conclude with practical tip and everyday connection
story_arc.reveal: Remove toast immediately or use a “hold‑open” function to stop the element’s lingering heat, turning a mundane breakfast into a lesson on thermal inertia.

ending_payoff: When the timer’s green light turns off, the toaster isn’t finished – its hot element keeps cooking the bread. Knowing this turns a frustrating burn into a simple habit: pull the toast out right when it pops, and you’ll never be surprised by a charred slice again.
